key_facts: A year-long government-commissioned review led by Alan Milburn, to be published on Tuesday, will recommend moving under-25s off the main sickness and disability benefits, including the health element of universal credit and personal independence payment (Pip), onto an allowance at the same basic rate as universal credit, with a possible new 'additional cost allowance' for some.

Milburn said the plans would not be 'pain-free' and would affect both existing and new claimants; he acknowledged some people could receive less financial support at the start of a claim, and the government is set to take the proposals into legislation in the new year.

The review is also expected to recommend billions of pounds of investment in youth employment support (work placements, job subsidies, one-to-one personal advisers), with a higher-rate new benefit for those with more severe disabilities who cannot work, and a carrot-and-stick model where benefits could be lost for not engaging with support.

Just under one million young people in the UK were not in education, employment or training (Neet) according to ONS data for April to June, a rise of 3% on the same period last year; the article says savings could take almost a decade to materialise.
importance_reason: Significant domestic welfare reform with fiscal implications, but no immediate direct market impact; largely a policy story.

A report last year found 8,310 converted flats in the pipeline in New York and 6,533 in Washington; Washington DC's goal is 15,000 new downtown residents by 2028, with tax cuts and eased planning rules supporting conversions.
